title: Isomorphic Strings
summary: You get two strings `s` and `t` of the same length. Decide whether `t` is `s` with its characters relabeled: every copy of a character in `s` must turn into the same character of `t`, and no two different characters may turn into the same one. A character may also stay as it is, and the order never changes.

examples.explanation: Each letter gets one partner: m → d, o → e, n → r. Both o's become e, and no two letters of s share a letter of t.
Both r and t would have to become p.

constraints: s and t may contain any ASCII characters: letters, digits, spaces and symbols

approaches.twist: Map each character of s to the character at the same position in t, keep a second map from t back to s, and fail when either map disagrees.
Check every pair of positions: two characters of s must be equal exactly when the characters of t at those positions are.
approaches.note: Works with O(1) extra space, but checking every pair of positions takes O(n²) time. The target is O(n).

approaches.twist: Rewrite each string as the list of first-appearance positions of its characters, and compare the two lists.
approaches.note: Works in O(n) time with a dict of first positions, but the two rewritten lists take O(n) extra space. The target is O(1).

signals.meaning: Each character of s is tied to one character of t. A dict remembers that pairing, so each later copy can be checked against it in O(1).
The pairing must be one-to-one, so check the other direction too: a second dict from t back to s, or a set of the characters of t already taken.
The strings line up position by position, so walk them together with zip(s, t).
At most 128 different characters can appear, so each dict holds at most 128 keys: O(1) space, however long the strings get.

constraintReading: len(s) can reach 5·10⁴, so checking every pair of positions means about 1.25·10⁹ comparisons: O(n²) is too slow. One pass with dict lookups is O(n). Only ASCII characters appear, so each dict holds at most 128 keys, which is O(1) space.

related.relation: Also compares two strings through a dict, but only the letter counts must agree, not which letter stands at each position.
